newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Govt support fading.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Govt support fading.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
A shiver of political reality ran up the coalition's spine this week.
One year into government, facing an opposition which Labor President Barry Jones admitted this week is in a "policy vacuum", the Howard government should be revelling in its impregnability.
But the latest Morgan Poll shows impregnability is a fleeting commodity in politics.

For the first time, the coalition's support dropped below the 47 percent primary vote level it received in last year's election -- from 49.5 percent on March 19 and 20 to 43.5 percent on March 25 and 26. That's an extraordinary six points deterioration in one polling period.

Pollster Gary Morgan attributed the entire fall to the Mal Colston affair, arguing that public perception was apportioning the blame for Senator Colston's apparent rorts across parliamentarians in general, weighted more heavily towards Liberals and National party MPs, who are seen to be defending the renegade senator.
Many Liberal MPs privately have been complaining for some time that they're all being lumped into the Colston basket.
Tim Fischer mentioned that publicly this week, showing the first cracks in the coalition's resolve to protect Colston in the hope his vote will help legislation through the Senate.
As noted here before, Fischer and his ramblings, sometimes bordering on the incoherent, should not be underestimated.
He carefully thinks through the purpose of his apparent stream of consciousness before offering himself to the media.
Each has a deliberate purpose.
In this case he had decided it was time the coalition cut the painter between the coalition and Colston.

The method was to tell ABC Radio's AM audience that there was "a lot of anger out there" in the electorate over the discrepancies in Colston's travel allowances and that taxpayers' money "must not be rorted."
But that hasn't been translated into action.
The government's still dragging the chain on taking the next logical step and calling in the Federal Police.
There seems little point in the delay.
Parliament is not sitting until Budget day -- May 13.
Colston's vote has no value during the recess.

The senator has until April 18 to reply to the latest batch of 27 discrepancies identified by the Department of Administrative Services. If the government dallies too long after receiving his explanation it will be inviting a greater backlash and resulting poll punishment.
But this is not to accept Gary Morgan's view that Colston is the government's only problem.
The euthanasia issue is also bubbling away in the community.
Indeed many Australians could well be asking the questions: How well served are we by our current crop of parliamentarians?
A broad brush view might well be that when MPs are not rorting their entitlements they are voting down an element of choice which the polls indicate is desired by around 70 percent of the population.
The letters pages of the newspapers have been full of the euthanasia debate with pro-euthanasia views dominating.
It seems the parliamentary vote is reversed in the general community.

The successful bill which crushed the Northern Territory's euthanasia legislation was sponsored by Kevin Andrews, a leading member of the coalition's Lyons forum, the conservative Christian group which has about 50 members.
Tasting victory through the Andrews bill, the forum is bound to have some big ideas for the future.
But they're not necessarily bound to be any more popular than the Andrews bill.
There's a cautionary tale here.
If the coalition leadership allows the Lyons forum to push various conservative barrows too often there could well be a political cost.
But John Howard's not likely to jump on the group too hard -- he's a known supporter.

And there's another unfavourable straw in the wind for the coalition. Kim Beazley's reshuffle, cunningly unveiled last Thursday after everyone had left Canberra for the Easter break, and John Howard had taken off for Singapore and China, holds some dangers for the Howard front bench.
The changes were derided by Tim Fischer as a Labor admission that it had failed to make any dent in the Howard team -- "a desperate attempt to regain credibility," he said.
But the promotion of two of the younger front benchers could have the government on the back foot.

Jenny Macklin's promotion to Social Security -- taking it from John Faulkner -- is recognition for her dogged work in the family services area where she has often had Family Services Minister Judi Moylan tied up, looking fragile, particularly over nursing homes.
Mark Latham's elevation to the key education and youth affairs portfolio will give Labor new impetus in this area.
Latham is hard-working, aggressive and articulate and will give Minister David Kemp a much harder time than did Peter Baldwin.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
